claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is primarily controlled by interface-mediated activation of dislocation sources.
Compositional complexity produces heterogeneous, locally varying energy barriers at interfaces.
Severe lattice distortion produces heterogeneous, locally varying energy barriers at interfaces.
Short-range chemical order produces heterogeneous, locally varying energy barriers at interfaces.
Interfacial barriers initially resist dislocation transfer but yield under sustained stress.
Yielding of interfacial barriers causes a gradual transition from elastic to plastic behavior through dislocation nucleation and transmission.
The starting multilayers have alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers with coherent interfaces.
The starting multilayers possess significant lattice distortion and local short-range chemical order.
Controlled annealing or adjustment of layer thickness can vary interfacial coherency.
Interface structure mediates the transition between deformation modes through the density and distribution of dislocation-nucleation sites.
Lattice mismatch, short-range order, and coherent versus semi-coherent boundary character modulate interfacial dislocation-nucleation sites.
Sustained loading causes local stress concentrations to build at chemically and structurally heterogeneous interfaces.
Once a critical stress is reached, dislocations nucleate and transmit across interfacial barriers, progressively accommodating plastic strain.
The severity of lattice distortion and short-range order directly influences the critical stress for dislocation nucleation and transmission.
Enhanced interface coherency or modifications that reduce local stress concentrations will delay the onset of plastic deformation relative to the baseline.
Enhanced interface coherency or reduced local stress concentrations will lower the creep rate relative to the baseline.
Disrupted or less coherent interfaces will activate dislocation sources earlier and produce faster, more pronounced deformation under otherwise identical loading.
The proposed mechanism is expected only in the nanoscale multilayer regime at creep-relevant temperatures.
At temperatures too low for sufficient dislocation activation, the proposed mechanism may not be observed.
At temperatures high enough for bulk diffusion to dominate, the proposed mechanism may not be observed.
